title: One page at a time: writing a story in a notebook
description: A notebook story asks for no audience, no likes and no deadline. One page a day is enough — and a story written slowly, by hand, belongs to its writer in a way typed drafts rarely do.

body.heading: Start smaller than the story
paragraphs: Do not begin with a plot. Begin with one page about one moment: a character opening a door, finding a strange key, hearing a noise in the attic. A single vivid scene is a promise you can keep tomorrow, when page two asks what happened next.

Write by hand if you can. Handwriting is slower than typing, and that slowness is a feature: sentences get thought about, crossings-out stay visible, and the notebook becomes a record of the story growing, not just the story.

body.heading: Keep the chain unbroken
paragraphs: One page a day sounds modest until you count: in a school term that is a short novel's worth of pages. The rule that makes it work is forgiving — a bad page still counts, because the habit being built is returning, not performing.
Keep the notebook private unless you choose to share it. Stories grow braver when nobody is watching, and you can always copy out the best pages later for an audience.

takeaway: One handwritten page a day, kept private and forgiven when it is bad, quietly adds up to a whole story.
